name: Southern Comfort
description: Whiskey, peach and spice, first mixed in a New Orleans bar in 1874 by a bartender who was tired of serving rough whiskey and decided to fix it rather than replace it. For decades it contained no whiskey at all; it does again now.
funFact: Martin Wilkes Heron originally called it Cuffs and Buttons, a joke on the fancier name of a rival drink, before settling on something more marketable.

serve.how: Over ice with a squeeze of lime, or long with lemonade. It is sweet enough that neat service is heavy going. In cocktails it does the work of both whiskey and sugar, which is why an Alabama Slammer needs neither.

composition.summary: Whiskey blended with peach, citrus and spice, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: American whiskey, reinstated in the 2010s after years of neutral spirit

composition.process: The original was a way of making cheap New Orleans whiskey drinkable, which is exactly what it still tastes like.

name: Ōkolehao
description: Distilled from the baked root of the ti plant, first made in Hawaii around 1790 by a shipwrecked Australian convict who saw what the islanders were fermenting and fetched a still. The name means iron bottom, after the shape of the pots.
funFact: Ti root was baked in the same underground imu ovens used for cooking pigs, which is where the faint smoke in traditional okolehao came from.

serve.how: Neat or over a single cube. Modern craft bottlings are clean enough to sip; older-style ones are earthier and work better in a tiki build where the root note can sit under lime and pineapple.

composition.summary: Baked ti root fermented and distilled, sometimes with cane or rice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cordyline fruticosa root, baked to convert its starch

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; originally an improvised ship's still

composition.process: Baking the root in an underground oven converts inulin to fermentable sugar, the same principle as roasting agave.

name: Canadian Rye
description: For most of a century Canadian whisky was called rye regardless of what was in it. A wave of distillers has since made the label honest, producing whiskies with real rye in the mash and the spice to prove it.
funFact: Canadian law lets distillers add up to 9.09% of another spirit, including wine or bourbon, which is why the category has so much latitude in flavour.

serve.glass: Glencairn neat, rocks glass on ice
serve.how: Neat for the rye-forward bottlings, which carry enough spice to hold up. On ice or in an Old Fashioned for the blends. Canadian rye's dill note makes it a distinctive base in a Manhattan.

composition.summary: Rye distilled and aged separately, then blended to a house style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, or rye blended with corn, wheat and barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column and pot, each grain distilled separately

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in Canada, in barrels no larger than 700 litres

composition.process: Distilling each grain separately and blending afterwards is the Canadian method and the source of its flexibility.

name: Screech
description: Newfoundland's rum, which is Jamaican in origin, bottled on the island, and surrounded by more ceremony than most spirits three times its price. The screech-in ritual involves kissing a cod and reciting a phrase in dialect.
funFact: The name is said to come from an American serviceman's reaction to his first mouthful during the Second World War, which was audible from outside.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or rocks glass with cola
serve.how: Neat as a shot during a screech-in, or long with cola the rest of the time. It is a dark, sweet rum without much complexity, and pretending otherwise is not part of the tradition.

composition.summary: Caribbean rum shipped in bulk and bottled in Newfoundland.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled in the Caribbean, blended and bottled in St John's

composition.process: Newfoundland traded salt cod to the Caribbean for rum for centuries, which is how a Jamaican spirit became a Canadian institution.

name: Maple Liqueur
description: Canadian whisky sweetened with maple syrup, which sounds like a novelty and turns out to be a genuinely good pairing. Quebec makes most of it, and Quebec makes most of the world's maple syrup, so the logic holds.
funFact: Quebec produces around seventy per cent of the world's maple syrup and maintains a strategic reserve of it in warehouses, which has been robbed at least once.

serve.how: Over ice, or poured into black coffee on a cold day. It is also good over vanilla ice cream and works in an Old Fashioned in place of both the whisky and the sugar.

composition.summary: Canadian whisky blended with pure maple syrup.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Pure maple syrup, typically Quebec grade

composition.process: Real syrup rather than maple flavouring is what separates the good bottles from the souvenir ones.

name: Charanda
description: Michoacán's protected cane spirit, distilled at altitude from cane grown in volcanic soil. Older than most Caribbean rum traditions and almost entirely unknown outside Mexico, where it has held a denomination since 2003.
funFact: The name comes from a Purépecha word for reddish soil, referring to the volcanic ground the cane grows in around Uruapan.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would approach a good rhum agricole. The mineral edge comes from the soil and gets lost under mixers, so save the mixing for the aged expressions.

composition.summary: Michoacán sugarcane, juice or molasses, fermented and distilled at altitude.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cane grown between 300 and 1,800 metres in Michoacán

composition.process: Distilling at altitude lowers the boiling point, which producers say gives a lighter, more aromatic spirit.

name: Comiteco
description: A Chiapas spirit made from fermented agave sap rather than roasted hearts, fortified and aged. It nearly died out entirely in the twentieth century and survives now through a handful of producers around Comitán.
funFact: Unlike tequila or mezcal it uses aguamiel, the sap tapped from a living agave, which is the same liquid that ferments into pulque.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature. It is sweeter and rounder than mezcal, closer to a light rum in weight, and the aged versions drink comfortably after a meal.

composition.summary: Agave sap fermented, distilled and blended with piloncillo, then aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguamiel from Agave americana, tapped from living plants

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, then blended with unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, typically one to three years

composition.process: Because the plant is tapped rather than harvested, it keeps producing sap for months before it dies.

name: Kahlúa
description: Coffee liqueur built on Veracruz arabica and Mexican cane spirit, made since 1936 and responsible for a disproportionate share of the world's dessert cocktails. Without it there is no White Russian and no Espresso Martini worth drinking.
funFact: The name comes from a Nahuatl phrase said to mean house of the Acolhua people, chosen by the founders for its local resonance.

serve.how: Over ice, or with cold milk or cream poured over it. In cocktails it is the sweet coffee half of a White Russian, an Espresso Martini or a Mudslide. Neat it is very sweet and best kept short.

composition.summary: Rum and neutral cane spirit blended with coffee extract, vanilla and sugar.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffee extracted and blended after distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The rum component is aged before blending

composition.process: The coffee is extracted rather than distilled, which keeps the roast character that distillation would strip.

name: Rompope
description: Egg, milk, sugar and cinnamon fortified with rum or cane spirit, invented in the convent kitchens of Puebla by nuns who had eggs to spare. Mexico's answer to advocaat, and a fixture of Christmas and every birthday in between.
funFact: The Santa Clara convent in Puebla is credited with the original, and the recipe was reportedly kept from the nuns themselves except for the one permitted to make it.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small glass, or poured over ice cream and flan. Mexicans drink it at Christmas and on Day of the Dead, and it is also spooned onto desserts rather than drunk.

composition.summary: Egg yolk, milk and sugar cooked together and fortified with spirit.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, milk, sugar, cinnamon, vanilla, sometimes almond

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the custard is cooked then fortified

composition.process: Cooking the custard before fortifying is what keeps it stable, and why homemade versions do not last long.

name: Xtabentún
description: A Yucatán liqueur of anise and fermented honey, the honey coming from bees that feed on the xtabentún morning glory. Mayan in origin, and the flower it depends on is mildly psychoactive to the bees if not to anyone else.
funFact: The Maya made a fermented honey drink called balché long before the Spanish arrived with anise and distillation, and the modern liqueur is a fusion of the two.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, or the local way: a shot of xtabentún poured into a cup of strong Yucatecan coffee. It also works over ice with soda when the Mérida heat makes anything else unthinkable.

composition.summary: Fermented honey blended with anise-flavoured rum or cane spirit.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Honey from xtabentún flowers, plus anise

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Honey fermented, then blended with the anise spirit

composition.process: The flower only grows in the Yucatán scrub, which is what ties the liqueur to the peninsula.

name: Damiana
description: A Baja California herb liqueur sold in a bottle shaped like an Incan fertility goddess, which tells you exactly what it has been marketed on for a century. Herbal, sweet, and the traditional base of the original Margarita, if you believe Baja.
funFact: Damiana has a long folk reputation as an aphrodisiac in Mexico, and the bottle shape has never been an accident.

serve.how: Over ice, or swapped in for triple sec in a Margarita, which is how Baja bars insist the drink was originally made. Neat it is sweet and herbal, closer to a chamomile liqueur than anything bitter.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with damiana leaf and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Turnera diffusa leaf, plus honey and herbs

composition.process: The shrub grows wild across the Baja peninsula and has been used in Mexican folk medicine since well before the Spanish.

name: Guatemalan Rum
description: Distilled from virgin cane honey rather than molasses and aged at over two thousand metres, where the thin cool air slows maturation dramatically. Ron Zacapa's solera system is what put the country on the map.
funFact: The high-altitude warehouse where Zacapa ages sits at 2,300 metres, and the ageing is slow enough that the solera numbers refer to years in the system rather than the youngest spirit.

serve.glass: Snifter or rocks glass with one cube
serve.how: Neat, or over a single large cube. These are sweet, heavily solera-aged rums, so treat them as you would a dessert spirit rather than a mixing rum. A twist of orange lifts the butterscotch.

composition.summary: Virgin cane honey fermented and column-distilled, then solera-aged at altitude.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera system in ex-bourbon, sherry and Pedro Ximénez casks at 2,300m

composition.process: Altitude and cool mountain air slow evaporation, which is why the spirit can sit in wood for so long without drying out.

name: Quetzalteca
description: Guatemala's everyday aguardiente, sold plain or in a run of fruit flavours, and named after the city of Quetzaltenango. It is on every shelf in the country and appears at every fiesta, wake and market day.
funFact: The fruit expressions, particularly tamarind and rosa de Jamaica, outsell the plain version in much of the country.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or mixed with fruit juice. It is an inexpensive, uncomplicated spirit and is drunk as one. The tamarind and hibiscus versions are the ones worth trying if you find them.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit, sometimes infused with fruit.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, to a high strength then cut

composition.process: The flavoured versions are infused after distillation, which is where most of the range now sits.

name: Honduran Aguardiente
description: Cane spirit with a touch of anise, of which Yuscarán is the name every Honduran knows. Cheap, clean and everywhere, and named after a colonial silver-mining town in the southern hills.
funFact: Yuscarán the town was built on silver, and the distillery that carries its name has outlasted the mines by well over a century.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with lime and soda. It is a working spirit rather than a sipping one, and Hondurans drink it in company rather than alone.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit lightly flavoured with anise.
composition.process: The anise is subtle enough that it reads as sweetness rather than as an aniseed spirit.

name: Cususa
description: Nicaraguan clandestine cane moonshine, distilled in the northern hills in improvised stills and sold with no label of any kind. Illegal, widespread, and occasionally very good.
funFact: Production is concentrated in the mountains around Estelí and Jinotega, where the sugar mills and the terrain both work in the distillers' favour.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a source you trust. Quality is entirely dependent on whether the maker cut the heads and tails properly, and there is no label to tell you.

composition.summary: Cane juice or panela fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Homemade pot stills, often single distillation

composition.process: Because it is unregulated, strength and safety vary enormously from one batch to the next.

name: Guaro
description: Costa Rica's state-produced cane spirit, deliberately kept low in strength and near-neutral in flavour so that it mixes with anything. Cacique is the national brand and has been a government monopoly product since 1850.
funFact: The state liquor factory was set up partly to stamp out home distilling, and the resulting monopoly funded public works for over a century.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or highball for a chiliguaro
serve.how: Cold shots, or in a chiliguaro: guaro with tomato juice, lime, hot sauce and salt, which is the national shot and far better than the description suggests. It also mixes cleanly with any fruit juice.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit distilled to near neutrality and cut to 30%.
composition.process: Keeping it neutral is a deliberate design choice: it was made to be mixed, not tasted.

name: Seco Herrerano
description: Panama's national spirit: sugarcane distilled three times to a clean, light, almost vodka-like spirit. Herrera province makes it, Panamanians drink it with milk, and almost nobody outside the country has heard of it.
funFact: Seco con leche, seco mixed with milk over ice, is a genuinely popular Panamanian serve and tastes considerably better than it reads.

serve.how: Over ice with coconut water, or the national serve of seco, milk and ice. It substitutes for vodka or white rum in almost anything, being cleaner than the first and lighter than the second.

composition.process: Three distillations strip out nearly all the cane character, which is what distinguishes it from rum.

name: Belizean Rum
description: Rum from Belizean molasses, of which One Barrel is the best known: a light, vanilla-heavy rum that has won more awards than a country of four hundred thousand people has any right to.
funFact: Travellers Liquors began as a roadside bar outside Belize City where the owner sold rum he had blended himself, and grew from there.

serve.how: Over ice, or long with soda and lime. The one-barrel style is light and vanilla-forward, which makes it a good daiquiri rum and an easy sipper over a single cube.

composition.summary: Belizean molasses fermented and column-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One year and upward in oak

composition.process: Belize's sugar industry is concentrated in the north, and the distilleries sit alongside the mills.

name: Rum Popo
description: Belize's Christmas eggnog liqueur, built on local rum with condensed milk, egg and nutmeg. Made at home in December in quantities that assume a large family and a long holiday.
funFact: Every Belizean family has its own ratio, and the arguments about how much rum belongs in it are a fixed part of the season.

serve.how: Cold from the fridge in a small glass, dusted with fresh nutmeg. It is thick and very sweet, so a small pour goes far. Homemade versions keep only a few days.

composition.summary: Local rum blended with egg, condensed milk and spice.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, condensed and evaporated milk, nutmeg, vanilla

composition.process: The condensed milk does the work that cream does in northern eggnog, and keeps better in the heat.
